_**Final Destination**_ is an American [horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_film "Horror film") [franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_franchise "Media franchise") owned by [Warner Bros. Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Entertainment "Warner Bros. Entertainment") through [New Line Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Line_Cinema "New Line Cinema"). It includes six films, ten novels, and two comic books. It is based on an unused [spec script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spec_script "Spec script") by [Jeffrey Reddick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Reddick "Jeffrey Reddick"), originally written for the television series _[The X-Files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_X-Files "The X-Files")_. The plots involve a group of people who escape death after a [visionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visionary "Visionary") has a [premonition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precognition "Precognition") of an [impending disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_casualty_incident "Mass casualty incident"). After avoiding their foretold fate, the survivors are later killed one by one in a series of bizarre accidents caused by an unseen force, often identified as [Death itself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personifications_of_death "Personifications of death"), which sets off intricate chains of events resembling [Rube Goldberg machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rube_Goldberg_machine "Rube Goldberg machine").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-1) The visionary then interprets omens in an effort to prevent further deaths.

In addition to the films, a novel series consisting of six original stories and novelizations of the first three films was published throughout 2005 and 2006 by [Black Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Flame_/(publisher/) "Black Flame (publisher)"). A one-shot comic book titled _Final Destination: Sacrifice_ was released alongside select DVDs of _[Final Destination 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination_3 "Final Destination 3")_ in 2006, and a comic book series titled _Final Destination: Spring Break_ was published by [Zenescope Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenescope_Entertainment "Zenescope Entertainment") in 2007.

The franchise has been praised for its innovative premise, with Death itself being a villain instead of the usual [slasher figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slasher_film "Slasher film"), and the creativity of the convoluted yet tense death sequences.

_Final Destination_ was written by [Jeffrey Reddick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Reddick "Jeffrey Reddick") after having "read a story about a woman who was on vacation and her mom called her and said, 'Don't take the flight tomorrow, I have a really bad feeling about it'". The woman switched flights, and the plane she was originally supposed to take crashed. Originally having written the script as an episode of _[The X-Files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_X-Files "The X-Files")_, Reddick decided to turn the script into a feature-length film at the behest of one of his [New Line Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Line_Cinema "New Line Cinema") colleagues. After developing the feature idea, New Line Cinema hired Reddick to write a screenplay; [James Wong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Wong_/(filmmaker/) "James Wong (filmmaker)") and [Glen Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Morgan "Glen Morgan") were later brought on board to write the shooting script, making alterations to comply with their standards. Jeffrey Reddick has sole story credit and shares screenplay credit with James Wong and Glen Morgan.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-2)

_Final Destination_ features high school student [Alex Browning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Browning "Alex Browning") ([Devon Sawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon_Sawa "Devon Sawa")), who boards Volée Airlines Flight 180 with his classmates for a field trip to [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). Before take-off, Alex has a premonition that the plane will explode in mid-air, killing everyone on board. When the events from his vision begin to repeat themselves in reality, he panics, and a fight breaks out, which leads to several passengers being left behind, including [Clear Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clear_Rivers "Clear Rivers") ([Ali Larter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Larter "Ali Larter")), Carter Horton ([Kerr Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerr_Smith "Kerr Smith")), Billy Hitchcock ([Seann William Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seann_William_Scott "Seann William Scott")), Valerie Lewton ([Kristen Cloke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristen_Cloke "Kristen Cloke")), Terry Chaney ([Amanda Detmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Detmer "Amanda Detmer")), and Tod Waggner ([Chad Donella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad_Donella "Chad Donella")), who witness the plane explode moments later. However, their survival caused them to cheat [Death itself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personifications_of_death "Personifications of death"), who also designed the Flight 180 explosion. As a result, Death created a new design to kill them one by one in bizarre accidents. Eventually, Alex, Clear and Carter travel to Paris to celebrate their survival, but when Alex suddenly witnesses Carter being crushed by a giant neon sign, they realize that Death is not finished with them.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-3)

### _Final Destination Bloodlines_ (2025)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Final_Destination&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Final Destination Bloodlines (2025)")\]

_Final Destination Bloodlines_ takes place in 1969 and 2024. In 1969, young Iris Campbell ([Brec Bassinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brec_Bassinger "Brec Bassinger")) and her fiancé Paul ([Max Lloyd-Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Lloyd-Jones "Max Lloyd-Jones")) go to the opening event of the Sky View Restaurant. She has a premonition that the tower will collapse, and as everybody runs for their lives, a series of chain reactions kills them. As the premonition ends, college student Stefani Reyes ([Kaitlyn Santa Juana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaitlyn_Santa_Juana "Kaitlyn Santa Juana")) is plagued, in 2024, by visions of her grandmother Iris's ([Gabrielle Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabrielle_Rose_/(actress/) "Gabrielle Rose (actress)")) premonition. She goes home to seek answers and is greeted by her father, Marty (Tinpo Lee), and her brother, Charlie ([Teo Briones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Briones "Teo Briones")). She later travels to Iris's cabin, where her grandmother hands her a notebook she created containing everything she has learned about Death's intent to kill all the Sky View survivors and their descendants. Iris allows Death to claim her to prove her claims to Stefani. Howard ([Alex Zahara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Zahara "Alex Zahara")) and Julia ([Anna Lore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Lore "Anna Lore")) are next to die. When Stefani and her remaining family members track down another survivor, "JB", at a hospital morgue, it is revealed that he is William Bludworth. Bludworth claims he is the last survivor of the Sky View disaster and will be the next to die once Stefani's family is killed. Stefani's cousins Erik ([Richard Harmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Harmon "Richard Harmon")) and Bobby ([Owen Joyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Joyner "Owen Joyner")) die in a freak mishap at the hospital. Charlie and Stefani head with their mother, Darlene ([Rya Kihlstedt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rya_Kihlstedt "Rya Kihlstedt")), to Iris's cabin so their mother may hide from Death. She is killed outside the cabin shortly before Charlie saves his sister from drowning by resuscitating her. A week later, while preparing for her brother's prom night, Stefani—whose heart did not stop when she drowned—and Charlie are crushed by logs that fly from a freight train that derails nearby.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-8)

Stein noted that the narrative potential remains open-ended, stating: "Death's work is never done. There are always more scores to settle."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-9) He acknowledged, though, that the creative process takes several years.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-10) Perry also expressed openness to continuing the franchise, noting that _Bloodlines_ has expanded the creative flexibility of the series.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-11) In August 2025, it was announced that a seventh movie in the franchise was in the works, with Taylor returning to write the script.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-12) In October 2025, it was announced that [Michiel Blanchart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michiel_Blanchart "Michiel Blanchart") would direct the seventh installment.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-13)

### Critical and public response

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Final_Destination&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Critical and public response")\]

The franchise has been praised for its innovative premise of the invisible abstract concept of Death killing people instead of a usual slasher killer, and the creativity of the films' death sequences.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-26)

Throughout 2005, publishing company [Black Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Flame_/(publisher/) "Black Flame (publisher)") released a series of _Final Destination_ books which faithfully follow the premise of the films, with each involving a group of people who find themselves targeted by Death after surviving a catastrophe of some sort due to a character experiencing a precognitive vision. Their first five novels all featured original stories, with the first novel, entitled _Dead Reckoning_, following a [punk rocker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") Jessica Golden who saves herself and several others from the collapse of Club Kitty in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), earning Death's ire.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-40) _Destination Zero_, also set in Los Angeles, has magazine employee Patricia Fuller and few others survive a train bombing and afterward, while being stalked by Death, Patti learns this is not the first time her family has been hunted by the entity.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-41) _End of the Line_ has a group of [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") [subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway") crash survivors, led by twins Danny and Louise King, trying to escape Death, who uses an unknowing agent to hasten its acquisition of the survivors.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-42) In _Dead Man's Hand_ a group meant to die in the crash of a [Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas_Valley "Las Vegas Valley") glass elevator are stalked by both Death and the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation"), the latter believing the group's savior Allie Goodwin-Gaines was responsible for the elevator crash.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-43) _Looks Could Kill_ has beautiful New York model Stephanie "Sherry" Pulaski stopping her friends from boarding a [yacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yacht "Yacht") when she has a vision of it exploding, but is left horribly disfigured and comatose by flying debris moments afterward when her vision comes true; eventually awakening the embittered Stephanie makes a deal with Death, aiding it in claiming her friends in exchange for having her good looks restored.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-44)

After the run of the original series of books, Black Flame released novelizations of the first three films in January 2006.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-46)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-47) Black Flame's last _Final Destination_ novel was _Death of the Senses_ released in mid-2006. Taking place in New York, the book has a homeless man named Jack Curtis saving policewoman Amy Tom from a maniac after having a vision of Amy's death; Amy's attacker is later revealed to be a serial killer who was meant to murder six other people (representing the first [five senses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense "Sense") and [a sixth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrasensory_perception "Extrasensory perception")) who Death begins targeting as Jack and Amy rush to find and warn the intended victims.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-48) It was, due to a printing error, only available for a short period of time before being recalled, leaving only a few copies in circulation. A tenth novel, titled _Wipeout_ and written by Alex Johnson, was planned, but cancelled; the book would have featured a pair of surfers and several others, after surviving a plane crash in [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"), being hunted by Death and the survivor of another disaster, an unstable soldier who had nearly died in an ambush in [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_/(2001%E2%80%93present/) "War in Afghanistan (2001–present)").[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-49)

The first _Final Destination_ comic book, titled _Sacrifice_, was published by [Zenescope Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenescope_Entertainment "Zenescope Entertainment") and came packaged with a limited edition DVD of _Final Destination 3_, sold exclusively at [Circuit City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_City_Corporation "Circuit City Corporation") stores in 2006. The premise of the story involves the survivor of a terrible accident and his friend Jim, who continually experiences images of other people's deaths, isolating himself from the rest of the world to escape the visions that torment him.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-50) In the same year, Zenescope later released a five issue miniseries, titled _Final Destination: Spring Break_, which involves a group led by Carly Hagan being stalked by Death after surviving a hotel fire and becoming stranded in [Cancún, Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canc%C3%BAn "Cancún"). The miniseries was later released in a trade paperback collection in 2007, which included the _Sacrifice_ comic as bonus content.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-51)

Three critical theories about the _Final Destination_ franchise have been discussed in scholarly works. It has been framed as a [postmodern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodernist_film "Postmodernist film") horror franchise that, like the [_Scream_ franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scream_/(franchise/) "Scream (franchise)"), self-consciously refers to the [history of horror cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_horror_films "History of horror films") and rewards viewers for their knowledge. Second, the films—particularly _[The Final Destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Final_Destination "The Final Destination")_ (2009) and _[Final Destination 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination_5 "Final Destination 5")_ (2011)—have been examined for their visual effects. Third, the franchise has been criticized for being cynical and reductive.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-B300-52) For example, film studies scholar Reynold Humphries dismisses the franchise as "obscurantist nonsense whose only 'idea' is that death is an agency that has a 'plan' for each of us".[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-53)

According to [media studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_studies "Media studies") scholar Eugenie Brinkema, _Final Destination_ films are characterized by their move away from the typical horror [antagonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antagonist "Antagonist") and toward the certainty and inevitability of death.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-54) This makes them inconsistent with most other horror films, which require a monster. _Final Destination_ films depart further from other horror films, even those aimed at teenagers, in that a family narrative is lacking, and there are no hauntings of any kind. As well, there is no sexuality—"neither the pursuit of pleasure in the slasher convention of easy bodily access nor the monstrosity of sexual difference".[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-B300-52) Brinkema argues the films are not about seeking pleasure like typical [slasher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slasher_film "Slasher film") films. Instead they are about the avoidance of pain and death; they are fundamentally "bitter ... paranoid, and sad" and display the inability of characters to feel pleasure.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-55) In these films, death becomes its own cause. The premonition of the roller coaster derailment in _Final Destination 3_ is without context or cause. The avoidance of death by some characters grounds the necessity of their deaths, specifically the order in which they would have died on the roller coaster.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-56) Thus, "Death's list" or "Death's design" is realized.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-B300-52) _Final Destination 3_ spends as much time interpreting deaths as displaying them. Wendy's close analysis of photographs allows her to understand the deaths, but is inevitably too late to save her friends.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-57) In the franchise's films, Brinkema says, "one must closely read to survive (for a spell), and yet reading changes absolutely nothing at all".[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-58) Thus, the characters "might as well" have stayed on the roller coaster.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-59)

Ian Conrich, a film studies scholar, argues the series marks a key departure from slasher norms in that death itself becomes the villain. _Final Destination_ films draw influences from slasher cinema, but the franchise's action sequences, including _Final Destination 3_'s roller coaster derailment, draw from [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film "Action film") and [disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster_film "Disaster film") cinema.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-C114-60) For Conrich, the franchise marks a new slasher film subgenre. Because the deaths are extremely violent and excessive, any number can happen at once, and all of them are inevitable, he calls the films "grand slashers".[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-C114-60) Other grand slashers include the films in the [_Saw_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saw_/(franchise/) "Saw (franchise)") and _[Cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cube_/(film_series/) "Cube (film series)")_ franchises.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-C114-60)

A notable feature of the _Final Destination_ films is the threshold or tipping-point logic of characters' deaths.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-61) Conrich frames the complex death sequences in _Final Destination_ films as "death games, contraptions or puzzles in which there are only losers". He compares the sequences to [Rube Goldberg machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rube_Goldberg_machines "Rube Goldberg machines"), the [Grand Guignol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Guignol "Grand Guignol"), and the _[Mouse Trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouse_Trap_/(board_game/) "Mouse Trap (board game)")_ board game.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-C115-62) Brinkema selects the deaths of Ashley and Ashlyn from _Final Destination 3_ as epitomizing the series' death sequences. The characters' deaths are brought about by "a series of neutral gestures, a set of constraints that will ultimately lead to their conflagratory ends"; these include the placing of a drink, looking through CDs, and an ill-chosen doorstop. The scene uses logics of temperature, color, and light to realize the characters' deaths and to allow Wendy to recognize the threat they face.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-Brinkema_303%E2%80%934-63) An example of the "literal tipping point" at which the characters can no longer escape occurs when a coat rack is knocked onto the tanning beds; it is blown by an air conditioning unit that is activated by the increasing heat.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-64) Conrich identifies the roller coaster derailment as an example of the franchise's focus on mobility in death sequences. He argues that theme park rides and horror cinema are mutually influential; the former draw from the frightening aspects of the latter, while the latter draw from the "theatrics and kinetics" of the former.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Destination#cite_note-C115-62)
